cards.explanation: The army is coming from Edom, from beyond the Sea. The messengers tell Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, “A vast army is coming against you from Edom, from beyond the Sea…” (2 Chronicles 20:2). They add that it's already in Hazazon-tamar, which is En-gedi. So this isn't a rumor from far away, friends. It's practically at the door, and I'd have burned a whole batch just hearing that news.

Jehoshaphat sets his face to seek the LORD. The text says he was alarmed, and right after that he “…set his face to seek the LORD.” Alarmed, but he still turned toward God first. He didn't stop at a plan, he went looking for God. That's a king who knows where to run first.

The answer is fast. After he sets his face to seek the LORD, Jehoshaphat proclaims a fast throughout Judah. The whole land is told to do this together. Every person in Judah has a reason to look up, not just the king.

The answer is False. The text says the people of Judah gathered to seek the LORD, and they came “…from all the cities of Judah to seek Him.” It's a whole kingdom, not one crowd from the capital. Jerusalem isn't the only city on that list, friends.

The answer is Abraham. Jehoshaphat prays that God gave this land forever to the descendants of Abraham, His friend. He says it right there in front of the assembly. I think that's a smart way to start when you're scared, friends.

The answer is that God would hear them and save them. Jehoshaphat repeats what the people said when they built the sanctuary: when they cried out in distress, “…You will hear us and save us.” That's what they were counting on, and he's holding that sentence up in prayer right now. Hear and save, friends, that's the whole answer.

The answer is False. Jehoshaphat says it plainly: “See how they are repaying us by coming to drive us out of the possession that You gave us as an inheritance.” Peace is the opposite of what he's describing. He's asking God to see how they're repaying Judah.

The answer is that they don't know what to do, but their eyes are on God. After saying they're powerless, Jehoshaphat says, “We do not know what to do, but our eyes are upon You.” A king with no plan and nothing to hide. I think that's one of the bravest sentences in this whole story, friends. He's not out of hope, he just knows where to look.

The answer is True. The text says all the men of Judah, “…with their wives and children and little ones…” were standing before the LORD. It's the whole community, not just the leaders. Nobody's watching this from the sidelines, friends. They're all there together.

The answer is God. Jahaziel, a Levite from Asaph's descendants, speaks after the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him. He says, “…the battle does not belong to you, but to God.” That takes the weight off the king and the whole crowd. They don't have to carry it.

The answer is to stand firm and see the LORD save them. Jahaziel says, “Take up your positions, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf…” They show up, stand firm and watch God save them. He also says, “You need not fight this battle.” Their job is to be there and trust.

The answer is to believe in the LORD and His prophets. As they set out, Jehoshaphat says, “Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be upheld; believe in His prophets, and you will succeed.” He talks about belief, and swords don't come up. That's the whole instruction, friends.

The answer is singers praising the LORD. Jehoshaphat appoints those who would sing to the LORD and praise the splendor of His holiness. They go out before the army, singing, “Give thanks to the LORD, for His loving devotion endures forever.” That's what's out front, friends.

The answer is that He sets ambushes against them. The text says, “The moment they began their shouts and praises, the LORD set ambushes against the men of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir…” The timing is right there in the verse. The praise begins, and the LORD acts, friends.

The answer is False. The text says that when they finished off the inhabitants of Seir, the Ammonites and Moabites “…helped to destroy one another.” They turned on each other instead of making peace. It's a hard verse.

The answer is only bodies lying on the ground. The men of Judah come to a place overlooking the wilderness and look for the vast army. What they find is “…only corpses lying on the ground; no one had escaped.” This part is heavy. The army they were afraid of isn't there anymore.

The answer is three. Judah gathers plunder for three days because there's so much of it. They found more than they could carry away. Then on the fourth day they assembled to bless the LORD. Three whole days of hauling, friends, and I'd want a nap by lunch.

The answer is True. On the fourth day, they assembled in the Valley of Beracah, where they blessed the LORD. After three days of gathering plunder, they stop and turn back to Him. The place was still called the Valley of Beracah when this was written.

The answer is True. They entered Jerusalem and went into the house of the LORD “…with harps, lyres, and trumpets.” They came back joyful, and the music came with them. The march that started with singers ends with instruments.

The answer is fear. The text says, “…the fear of God came upon all the kingdoms of the lands when they heard that the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel.” Every kingdom of the lands hears what the LORD did. The news reaches them, and the fear of God comes upon them.

The answer is that his kingdom is at peace with rest on every side. The text says Jehoshaphat's kingdom was at peace, “…for his God had given him rest on every side.” That comes right after the fear of God fell on the kingdoms. The rest came from his God, and it covered every side.

The answer is that Jehoshaphat allied himself with Ahaziah. Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah, a prophet, says, “Because you have allied yourself with Ahaziah, the LORD has destroyed your works.” Ahaziah was king of Israel, and the text says he acted wickedly. The reason is right there in the prophet's own words. It's a sad ending after such a great victory, friends.
